hook.text: Here are two groups of forty people, and group B scores more than three and a half points higher.

same.text: Here's the catch. Both groups came from the SAME process. There's no real difference at all.

again.text: So draw both groups again... and this time, A comes out ahead, by one point seven.

more.text: Again, and again. By about two, then three, then one.

free.text: Five draws, and the gap is never zero. Randomness makes differences for free.

luck.text: So before you believe any gap, ask one question... could this just be luck?

trend.text: Noise makes trends, too. Here are two years of a monthly metric.

fell.text: Over the last six months, it fell almost twelve points. Something must have happened... right?

flat.text: Nothing did. Every month is a hundred, plus random noise. The trend was never there.

process.text: Behind every dataset is a process like this one. Customers deciding, machines running, demand rising and falling.

output.text: You never see the process itself. You only see what comes out of it... signal, plus noise.

signal.text: The signal is the stable part, here that flat hundred. The noise is everything that wobbles around it.

job.text: Statistics is how you find the signal through the noise.

slice.text: And the numbers you get are only ever a slice... of something much bigger.

survey.text: Say you survey five hundred of your three hundred thousand customers.

exact.text: That tells you exactly what those five hundred said. But your question is about all three hundred thousand.

names.text: Everyone you care about is the population. The part you saw is the sample... here, one customer in six hundred.

list.text: And often, the population isn't even a list. It's every checkout a design will ever see, and most of them haven't happened yet.

parameter.text: A number that describes the population is a parameter. It's fixed... but you can't see it.

statistic.text: A number you compute from the sample is a statistic. You can see it, but it moves.

letters.text: Parameters get Greek letters, like mu for a mean. Statistics get Latin ones, like x-bar.

cheat.text: In code, we can cheat and know the truth. Build a population with a mean of a hundred, and sample fifty.

miss.text: Their average is a hundred and one point four. Close, but not on it.

price.text: That miss isn't a mistake. It's the price of seeing only part.

twenty.text: Now draw fifty more, and fifty more. Twenty samples give twenty different answers.

moves.text: The parameter never moved. Only the statistic did.

variable.text: That makes a statistic a random variable, with a center and a spread of its own.

points.text: So think in distributions, not points. Any one average is a single draw from that spread.

kind.text: But before you summarize a sample at all... you need to know what KIND of number you're holding.

flavors.text: Take a survey that stores favorite ice cream flavors as numbers. One is vanilla, two is chocolate, three is strawberry.

average.text: Ten people answer. Average the column, and you get one point eight.

none.text: There is no flavor one point eight. The math ran fine... but those numbers were labels, not quantities.

mode.text: The honest summary is the most common answer. Vanilla.

kinds.text: So every column is one of two kinds. Categorical data says which group. Numerical data says how much, or how many.

labels.text: Labels split again. Nominal ones have no order, like countries. Ordinal ones do, like shirt sizes, but the gaps between them can be uneven.

numbers.text: Numbers split into counts, like logins, and measurements, like price.

trap.text: The dangerous columns look numerical, but aren't. Take four zip codes.

pandas.text: pandas stores them as integers, and averages them without a word. Forty-eight thousand, seven hundred and fifty-five.

place.text: That isn't a place. It's the average of four labels.

double.text: One test catches it. Would doubling the value mean anything? Double a price, and it costs twice as much. Double a zip code... and you get nonsense.

dtype.text: The data type only says how a number is stored. What it means is your call.

decides.text: And that call decides what you're allowed to do. Labels get counts and the most common value. Ranks get a median. Quantities get a mean.

tests.text: Later, it picks the test, too. Two categorical columns call for a chi-square test. A number compared across two groups, a t-test.

next.text: And even a real quantity can mislead. Is its average the typical value? Not always... skew can pull it off center.

trend-in.text: And it isn't only gaps between groups.

parameter-in.text: So it helps to name the numbers on each side.

twenty-in.text: So how big is that miss, usually? One sample can't tell you.

flavors-in.text: Here's what goes wrong when you don't.

kinds-in.text: The computer couldn't tell a label from a quantity. That part is up to you.

trap-in.text: Most columns tell you plainly which kind they are. A few don't.
